details:
**"The Overcoat"**
Gogol's most famous short story, about Akaky Akakievich, a meek St. Petersburg government copyist. He saves for a new overcoat, which is stolen by robbers on his way home from a party held to celebrate it. He dies after being berated by an official, and his ghost then haunts the city, stealing coats.

**Akaky Akakievich**
The protagonist of "The Overcoat," a lowly clerk who loves copying documents. The story opens by describing "a certain official" in "a certain department." When colleagues mock him, he cries out "I am your brother," which makes a young official ashamed of joining in the teasing.

**Petrovich the tailor**
The one-eyed tailor in "The Overcoat" who refuses to patch Akaky's worn-out coat and instead makes him a new one, using cat fur for the collar because marten is too expensive.

**The "Person of Consequence" (Important Person)**
The pompous high official Akaky turns to for help after his coat is stolen. The official scolds him so harshly that Akaky falls ill and dies. Akaky's ghost later attacks this official and takes his coat, after which the ghost stops appearing.

**"The Nose"**
An absurd story in which Major Kovalyov, a collegiate assessor, wakes up to find his nose missing. The nose appears around St. Petersburg in the gold-braided uniform of a State Councilor, outranking its owner, and is later caught trying to leave for Riga by stagecoach with a forged passport. It eventually reappears on Kovalyov's face.

**Ivan Yakovlevich the barber**
The barber in "The Nose" who finds Kovalyov's nose baked inside a loaf of bread at breakfast. He tries to get rid of it by dropping it into the Neva River from a bridge, which draws a policeman's suspicion. Kovalyov had earlier complained that the barber's hands smelled, prompting the reply, "But why should they stink?"

**Major Kovalyov and Madame Podtochina**
Platon Kuzmich Kovalyov is the vain, rank-obsessed owner of the nose. He suspects that Madame Podtochina, who wanted him to marry her daughter, used witchcraft to take his nose.

**Dead Souls**
Gogol's unfinished novel, the second part of which survives only in fragments. In it, the swindler Pavel Ivanovich Chichikov travels through the provinces buying the legal titles to dead serfs who are still listed on the census rolls, so he can use them as collateral. The surviving text ends mid-sentence during a prince's speech condemning corruption.

**Chichikov's landowners, Captain Kopeikin, and the troika**
In Dead Souls, Chichikov buys dead souls from grotesque landowners such as the miser Plyushkin and the bearish Sobakevich. Townspeople speculate that he may be Napoleon in disguise or the legendary disabled veteran Captain Kopeikin. Part one ends by comparing Russia to a speeding troika (a sled drawn by three horses). In the second part, Chichikov buys an estate from Khlobuyev.

**The Inspector General (The Government Inspector)**
Gogol's satirical comedy in which the corrupt officials of a provincial town mistake the penniless traveler Khlestakov for a government inspector traveling incognito. They shower him with bribes, and he proposes to the mayor's daughter Maria before leaving. A letter he sends to the postmaster mocking the townspeople is opened and read aloud. Other clues include the mayor's order to hang Latin signs above hospital beds and a non-commissioned officer's widow who supposedly "flogged herself."

**"Diary of a Madman"**
A story told through the diary of Poprishchin, a minor clerk who slides into insanity. He reads letters between the dogs Medji and Fidele, worries that the earth will sit on the moon, and finally decides he is the heir to the Spanish throne, signing his name "Ferdinand VIII." It appeared in Gogol's collection Arabesques.

**"Nevsky Prospekt"**
A story contrasting two men who follow women along St. Petersburg's main avenue. The idealistic painter Piskarev follows a beautiful dark-haired woman who turns out to be a prostitute, and after she rejects his attempt to reform her he slits his throat. The shallow Lieutenant Pirogov follows the wife of a German tinsmith, is beaten for it, and soon consoles himself with puff pastries.

**Evenings on a Farm Near Dikanka**
Gogol's first successful collection of Ukrainian folk tales, narrated by the beekeeper Rudy Panko. It includes "St. John's Eve," "A May Night," "Christmas Eve" (in which the blacksmith Vakula rides the devil to St. Petersburg to get the tsaritsa's slippers for the village beauty Oksana), "A Terrible Vengeance" (with Danilo, Katerina, and an evil sorcerer by the Dnieper), and "The Enchanted Spot."

**"St. John's Eve"**
A story in the Dikanka collection in which Petro searches for a fern that blooms only on Kupala Night to find treasure. The witch guarding the treasure makes him behead the child Ivas to get it, and the devil eventually carries Petro off.

**"Viy"**
A horror story from the Mirgorod collection in which the seminary student and philosopher Khoma Brut (Thomas) must read prayers over the corpse of a witch for three nights. On the third night she summons the title demon, the Viy, whose gaze reveals Khoma, and he dies of fright.
